appearance: Weld does not penetrate the joint fully, just on the surface. Cross-section shows bead sitting on top with an unfused gap visible in the joint below.
causes: Incorrect welding technique (CTWD too long, arc not on leading edge, wrong gun angle).
remedies: Maintain 1/2" or less CTWD, keep arc on leading edge of weld puddle, hold MIG Gun at proper angles.
Reduce travel speed / increase weld current.
Bevel thick workpieces, allow slight gap, weld in several passes.

appearance: Weld droops on top and underneath, or falls through entirely, making a hole. Cross-section shows deep, sagging, rounded penetration well past the joint.
remedies: Reduce wire feed speed / decrease weld current.
Increase travel speed and keep it steady.

appearance: Workpiece plates appear angled/bent at the weld joint rather than flat/coplanar, seen in profile view.
remedies: Make tack welds to hold workpieces.
Weld a small portion and allow to cool before proceeding.

appearance: Gaps present between weld and previous bead or between weld and workpiece, visible at the upper shoulders and bottom tip of the weld profile.
remedies: Place stringer bead at correct place in joint.
Adjust workpiece position or weld angle to permit proper welding to bottom of piece.
Pause briefly at sides during weave bead.
Keep arc on leading edge of weld puddle.
Hold MIG Gun at proper angles.
Clean workpiece down to bare metal.

appearance: Small cavities or holes in the bead — visible as scattered light/white speckled dots along and beside the rippled weld bead in top view.
remedies: Check that polarity is set correctly for type of welding.
Increase flow of gas, clean nozzle, maintain proper CTWD.
Use shielding gas recommended by wire supplier.
Clean workpiece down to bare metal; keep wire clean and free from oil, coatings, residues.

appearance: Fine spatter is normal; grainy, large spatter is a problem — dense dark speckled granules scattered along both sides of the bead in top view.
remedies: Clean workpiece down to bare metal; keep wire clean and free from oil, coatings, residues.
Check that polarity is set correctly for type of welding.
Increase flow of gas, clean nozzle, maintain proper CTWD.

appearance: Bead wanders/curves left and right along its length instead of running straight, seen in top view.
remedies: Use two hands or rest hand on steady surface.

appearance: Base material melts away, leaving a hole in the weld — visible as a distinct blown-out white/irregular hole in the bead track in top view.
remedies: Reduce current and/or wire feed speed.
Increase travel speed and ensure that travel speed is kept steady.

appearance: Weld does not contact the joint fully, just on the surface. Cross-section shows bead sitting on top with an unfused gap in the joint below.
remedies: Keep arc on leading edge of weld puddle, hold torch at proper angles.
Slow down so fill material has time to melt into the weld location; increase current.
Bevel thick workpieces, allow slight gap, weld in several passes.

appearance: Weld droops on top and underneath or falls through entirely, making a hole. Cross-section shows deep sagging penetration.
remedies: Increase welding speed and ensure that welding speed is kept steady.

appearance: Photo shows a narrow, ropey, poorly-fused-looking bead with rough, piled texture, compared to the Good Weld reference bead.
Photo shows a wide, flat, splashy bead with irregular wavy/frayed edges and a burned, washed-out look.

defect: Weld Speed Too Fast (Stick example weld)
appearance: Photo shows a thin, narrow, widely-spaced ripple bead with understated build-up.

defect: Weld Speed Too Slow (Stick example weld)
appearance: Photo shows a wide, heavy bead with tightly bunched ripples and excess pooled material.

defect: Arc Length Too Short (Stick example weld)
appearance: Photo shows a narrow bead with small tight ripples and some irregular buildup.
causes: Arc length too short (electrode held too close to workpiece).

defect: Arc Length Too Long (Stick example weld)
appearance: Photo shows a wide, rough, spattery bead with an irregular blotchy surface texture.
causes: Arc length too long (electrode held too far from workpiece).
